unit.title: Troubleshoot and repair basic electrical/electronic apparatus

summary: This unit teaches you to find and repair faults in small mains appliances and simple battery-powered electronic circuits. You will learn a logical fault-finding method, how to use a multimeter and an insulation resistance tester for dead tests, how heating appliances, cords and common electronic parts work and fail, and how to solder and desolder. You will also learn to test a repair, deal with the customer and keep records.

blocks.p: This unit is about repair work at the bench: small appliances such as kettles, irons, toasters, rice cookers, lamps and hair dryers, and small electronic items such as battery chargers, power adapters and battery-powered circuit boards. It is for Level 2 trainees who work under supervision. You will find most faults with **dead tests**, with the item unplugged or its battery removed, because that is the safe way to work at this level.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Work safely at the repair bench
Unplug the item and keep the plug in view, isolate fixed equipment, discharge capacitors, solder safely, protect parts from static, and leave mains testing to the instructor.
Find out about the fault
Ask the customer what happens, when it started and what they noticed (a smell, a bang, water, a drop), and write it on the job card.
Use test instruments correctly
Set a multimeter for resistance, continuity, diode test, voltage and current, connect it the right way, and read the display, including 'OL'. Use an insulation resistance tester under supervision.
Follow a logical fault-finding method
Inspect first, then test in order (for example with the half-split method), and find the cause, not just the failed part.
Test and replace the parts of mains appliances
Cords, plugs, switches, thermostats, thermal fuses, elements and lampholders: test each one dead and fit a correct replacement.
Test and replace electronic components
Resistors, diodes, LEDs, capacitors, fuses and transformers on a circuit board; read colour codes and fit polarised parts the right way round.
Solder and desolder
Remove a part without lifting the tracks, and make a smooth, shiny joint with no bridges.
Test the repair
Earth continuity and insulation resistance on a mains appliance; correct battery polarity on an electronic circuit; a function test by the instructor on the protected test bench.
Deal with the customer and keep records
Explain the fault and the cost, let the customer decide, complete the repair record, and put e-waste in the right place.

ul: JPS supplies **110 V and 220 V at 50 Hz**. Most small appliances are 110–120 V. Water heaters, cookers, some ovens and large air-conditioners are 220 V. Read the rating plate before you test or replace anything.

Many appliances sold in Jamaica are made for the US market: 120 V, 60 Hz, with US-style plugs (two flat blades, often with a round grounding pin). Others are made for British or other markets. Check the plate and the plug.

The rating plate shows the voltage, the frequency, the power in watts (W), the model number and often a double-insulated symbol (a square inside a square). Copy these onto the job card before you start.

blocks.note: A 110–120 V appliance plugged into a 220 V outlet by mistake gets about twice its rated voltage and is usually badly burnt inside: element, motor, thermal fuse or circuit board. When a customer says an item 'blew' the moment it was plugged in somewhere new, ask which outlet it was plugged into.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Read the sections in order: they follow a real repair, from safety to handing the item back. Then try the practice test and read every explanation, even when you get the question right. Your instructor will show you the Centre's meters, testers and protected test bench.
Most repair work is done on equipment that is normally connected to the mains, so the first job is always to make it safe. At Level 2 you do not work on anything while it is connected to the mains.

blocks.h: Make it safe before you open it

head: Equipment
How to make it safe
rows: Plug-in appliance (kettle, lamp, iron, charger)
Unplug it at the outlet and keep the plug on the bench where you can see it, so nobody plugs it in while you work. Switching off at its own switch is not enough.
Fixed (wired-in) equipment, such as a water heater or a wall fan
Isolate at the breaker or isolator, lock off with your own padlock, fix a tag, and prove dead with a tester that you prove works before and after. Your supervisor leads this.
Battery-powered item
Take out the batteries or disconnect the battery clip before resistance tests or soldering.
Item with large capacitors (power supplies, motors with capacitors)
Capacitors can stay charged after unplugging. Discharge them with the Centre's resistor discharge tool, as the instructor shows you, then check with a meter on DC volts that they are empty.

blocks.note: Never work on a mains appliance while it is plugged in, and never plug in an appliance with its case open. At Level 2, any test with the mains switched on is done by the instructor on the Centre's protected test bench.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: **Microwave ovens.** They contain a high-voltage capacitor that can hold a charge of thousands of volts after the oven is unplugged, enough to kill. Leave them to trained, authorised technicians.
**The inside of switch-mode chargers and adapters**, unless the instructor tells you to and shows you how to discharge them (see the section on electronic components).
**Refrigerators, freezers and air-conditioners.** Their sealed gas systems are for refrigeration technicians.
**Anything that has been in a fire or a flood**, until the instructor has looked at it.

head: Hazard
How to control it
rows: Soldering iron tip (often 320–370 °C)
Keep the iron in its stand when you are not using it, never lay it on the bench, and switch it off when you leave.
Solder and flux fumes
Use fume extraction or a well-ventilated bench, and keep your face out of the smoke.
Lead in solder
Wash your hands after soldering and before eating or drinking. No food or drink at the bench.
Flying wire ends and solder splashes
Wear safety glasses when cutting leads, stripping wire and soldering. Point leads down when you cut them.
Static electricity
Wear an anti-static wrist strap and work on an anti-static mat when handling chips and transistors.
Sharp edges and hot parts
Take care with metal cases and heating parts; let hot parts cool before you touch them.
The insulation resistance tester
It gives 500 V DC. Warn people nearby, keep your hands off the item and the probes during the test, and let the tester discharge the item afterwards.
Batteries
Do not short-circuit them: a shorted battery gets very hot. Handle swollen or leaking batteries with gloves and keep them away from heat.

blocks.note: Keep the bench dry, tidy and well lit. Put screws and small parts in a labelled tray, keep drinks away, and clear off-cuts as you go. Most bench accidents start with clutter.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: You do not need a lot of theory to find most faults, but you do need these few ideas. They let you work out what a meter should read **before** you measure, so that you know at once whether a part is good.

Resistance

How strongly a part opposes the current. A heating element has a fairly low resistance; good insulation has a very high one.
Power

How fast energy is used. A 1000 W iron uses energy ten times as fast as a 100 W fan.

blocks.h: Ohm's law and the power formula

blocks.p: **Ohm's law: V = I × R.** Rearranged, I = V ÷ R and R = V ÷ I. **Power: P = V × I.** Putting the two together gives a formula you will use often at the bench: **R = V × V ÷ P**. It tells you what a heating element should read on the ohms range.

ul: **Example 1.** A 9 V battery circuit has a total resistance of 450 Ω. I = 9 ÷ 450 = 0.02 A = 20 mA.
**Example 2.** A 110 V iron is rated 1200 W. Its element should read R = 110 × 110 ÷ 1200 = 12 100 ÷ 1200 ≈ 10 Ω. It draws I = 1200 ÷ 110 ≈ 11 A.

**Example 3.** A small 12 V lamp draws 0.5 A. P = 12 × 0.5 = 6 W, and its resistance when lit is R = 12 ÷ 0.5 = 24 Ω. Measured cold it reads much lower, often about a tenth of that, because a filament's resistance rises greatly when it is white-hot.

blocks.h: What a heating element should read

head: Rating on the plate
Resistance worked out (R = V × V ÷ P)
rows: About 40 Ω
About 20 Ω
About 12 Ω
About 8 Ω
About 24 Ω
About 16 Ω

blocks.note: Elements read a little lower cold than the figure you work out, because their resistance rises slightly as they heat up. A reading close to the figure means the element is whole. **OL** means it is broken. A reading far below the figure can mean shorted turns or the wrong element.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: **Series**: parts one after another, so the same current flows through each. Resistances add: two 100 Ω resistors in series make 200 Ω. The supply voltage is shared between them.

**Parallel**: parts side by side across the same two points, so each gets the full voltage. The total resistance is less than the smallest one. Two equal resistors in parallel give half the value of one. For two resistors, R = (R1 × R2) ÷ (R1 + R2).

blocks.note: This is why you lift one leg of a part before you measure it on a board. Other parts connected across it give the meter extra paths, so the reading comes out lower than the part's real value.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: **AC** (alternating current) changes direction many times each second: the JPS supply alternates 50 times a second (50 Hz). **DC** (direct current) flows one way only: it comes from batteries and adapters and is used inside electronic circuits. Many electronic items take AC from the mains and change it to low-voltage DC in a power supply.

blocks.p: Your main instrument is the digital multimeter. You will also use an insulation resistance tester. Check every instrument before use: the case, the leads and probes (no cracks or bare metal) and the battery. Use a meter whose category (CAT) and voltage ratings suit the work; the Centre will tell you which meters to use.

ul: **COM**: the black lead, used for every measurement.
**VΩ**: the red lead, for volts, ohms, continuity and diode test.
**mA** and **10 A** (or 20 A): the red lead, for current only. These sockets are fused inside the meter.

**After measuring current, move the red lead back to the VΩ socket at once.** On the current sockets the meter has almost no resistance. If you then touch it across a voltage it acts as a short circuit: the meter's fuse blows, or the meter can flash over in your hand.

flow: Make sure the item is unplugged or its battery is out, and capacitors are discharged
Set the Ω range (on a manual meter, the lowest range above the value you expect)
Touch the leads together: the meter should read close to 0 Ω (note the lead resistance, often 0.1 to 0.5 Ω)
Measure across the part, lifting one leg if other parts are connected across it
Compare the reading with the value you worked out, the marked value or the maker's figure

ul: **OL** (over limit) on the ohms range means the resistance is too high to measure: an open circuit, or a value above the range you chose.
A minus sign on a DC volts reading means the leads are the wrong way round. The size of the reading is still correct.
Check the unit shown: Ω, kΩ or MΩ. A reading of 1.2 with kΩ showing is 1200 Ω.
A reading that keeps changing as you move a cord or tap a board points to an intermittent fault.

blocks.p: An insulation resistance tester applies a high DC test voltage, usually **500 V** for 110 V and 220 V equipment, and shows the resistance of the insulation in megohms (MΩ). Good insulation gives a **high** reading. A low reading means current can leak from the live parts to the case: the cause of tripping GFCIs and of shocks.

head: Appliance
How the test is made
rows: Metal-cased, with an earth pin (Class I)
Join the line and neutral pins together, switch the appliance ON so that the whole circuit is included, and test from the joined pins to the earth pin.
Double-insulated, square inside a square (Class II)
Test from the joined line and neutral pins to any metal you can touch on the outside, such as screws, a chuck or a metal trim.

blocks.note: The tester gives 500 V DC. Warn people nearby, keep your hands off the item and the probes during the test, and let the tester discharge the item afterwards. Some appliances with electronic controls can be damaged by 500 V or give a falsely low reading: follow the instructor, who may use 250 V or a different test.

blocks.p: Good technicians do not guess and swap parts until something works. They follow the same steps every time. It saves time and parts, and it is safer.

flow: Collect information from the customer and the job card
Make it safe: unplug, keep the plug in view, remove batteries, discharge capacitors
Inspect by eye, outside and then inside
Test dead, in a logical order
Find the faulty part
Find why it failed
Repair with a correct part
Test the repair
Record the work and hand over

ul: What does it do, or not do? Is it completely dead, or does part of it work (a lamp, a fan, a display)?
When did the fault start, and did anything happen first: a smell, smoke, a bang, a drop, water, a power cut or a storm?
Is the fault there all the time, or does it come and go?
What was it plugged into? Was it moved to a new outlet?
Has anyone else tried to repair it? Is it still under the maker's warranty? Opening it may end the warranty, so tell the customer first.
Write the customer's description on the job card in their own words.

blocks.h: 2 and 3. Make it safe, then look

blocks.p: Many faults can be seen or smelt. Before you test anything, look at the plug (bent or burnt pins, a cracked body), the cord (cuts, crushing, the outer sheath pulled out of the cord grip) and the case (cracks, melting, water marks). Then open it and look for burnt or broken wires, loose terminals, brown or black marks, swollen capacitors, cracked joints, rust, insects, and signs that someone has been inside before.

Follow the path of the current, from the plug to the load and back. For a simple appliance, test the cord, then the switch, then the thermostat and the safety devices, then the load. Write each result down as you go.

When there are many points to test, start in the **middle** of the circuit. If the result there is good, the fault is in the second half; if not, it is in the first half. Then test in the middle of the bad half, and so on. Each test halves the number of places where the fault can be.

blocks.note: **Example.** A battery LED board has eight test points, from the battery clip to the last LED. Instead of testing each point in turn, you test at point 4: the voltage is correct, so points 1 to 4 are good. You test at point 6: no voltage. The fault is between points 4 and 6, and one more test at point 5 finds it. Three tests instead of up to eight.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Flex the cord along its length while the meter is on continuity. A reading that drops out shows the break, often near the plug or where the cord enters the appliance.
Gently press or tap the board with an insulated tool while you watch a reading.
Look closely at the joints with a magnifier. Cracked rings round leads (dry joints) are common at heavy parts, connectors and battery terminals.
Some faults appear only when a part is warm. Your instructor may let you warm it gently with a hair dryer while you watch a dead-test reading.

sections.title: Mains appliances: cords, switches and heating parts

blocks.p: Most small appliances turn electricity into heat (kettles, irons, toasters, rice cookers, hair dryers), light (lamps) or movement (fans, blenders). Heating appliances are the most common repairs at Level 2.

blocks.h: How a heating appliance is wired

On/off switch, in the line
Thermostat: holds the temperature
Thermal fuse or cut-out: the safety backstop
Element: makes the heat
Back to the neutral

blocks.p: A pilot lamp (a small neon with a resistor, or an LED) is usually connected across the element, so it lights when the element has power. The earth conductor goes to the metal body, not through the circuit.

blocks.p: Many thermostats use a **bimetallic strip**: two metals bonded together that expand by different amounts when heated, so the strip bends and opens the contacts. As it cools it straightens and closes them again. Turning the dial changes how far the strip must bend. Some ovens and water heaters use a capillary thermostat instead. Many rice cookers use a magnet under the pot that lets go when the pot gets hotter than boiling water, after the water has gone, and this switches the cooker from 'cook' to 'warm'.

ul: A **thermal fuse** is marked with its operating temperature (for example 'Tf 184 °C') and its current and voltage ratings. Replace it only with one of the same type, temperature and current rating.
Thermal fuses are usually **crimped** into the circuit with the correct connectors, not soldered: the heat of soldering can open them. Refit the heat-resistant sleeve that covered the old one.
A thermal fuse is the last line of protection. If it has opened, something let the appliance overheat: find it.

blocks.p: Most appliances in Jamaica have US-style plugs. On a two-pin **polarised** plug the **wider blade is the neutral** and the narrower blade is the line, so the switch and any fuse are always in the line conductor. A three-pin plug adds a round **grounding (earth) pin**.

head: Conductor
US-style cord
IEC (British and European) cord

Black; on flat two-core cord, the smooth side
Brown
Neutral
White; on flat two-core cord, the side with ribs or a stripe
Blue

blocks.note: Colours on old cords may be faded, or may have been wired wrongly. Confirm which conductor goes to which pin with a continuity test before you connect anything.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Unplug the appliance and keep the plug in view
Note or photograph how the old cord is connected, then remove it
Choose a new cord of the same type, with the same number of cores and the same or a higher current rating
Pass it through the cord grip or grommet; strip the outer sheath only so far that the grip clamps on the sheath
Strip each conductor to the length its terminal needs, without nicking the strands; crimp on terminals where they were used
Connect line, neutral and earth to the right terminals, leaving the earth conductor a little longer than the others
Tighten the terminals and the cord grip, and route the wires away from hot parts and sharp edges
Fit or check the plug, wired the same way, then do the dead tests

ul: The earth conductor is left a little longer so that, if the cord is ever pulled hard, the line and neutral pull tight and break first and the earth is the last to come off.
Never tie a knot in a cord to hold it, and never use tape in place of a cord grip.
A metal-cased appliance needs a **three-core** cord. A two-core cord is used only on a double-insulated appliance (square inside a square), and only where the old cord was two-core.

blocks.note: Many appliances here are made for the US market and rated 120 V, 60 Hz. Heating appliances work normally on JPS's 50 Hz. Items with motors or transformers marked '60 Hz only' may run a little hotter on 50 Hz, and motors a little slower. Note the plate when you look for the cause of an overheating fault.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A **printed circuit board (PCB)** holds the parts and joins them with thin copper **tracks** (traces). Each part's leads are soldered to copper **pads**. On through-hole boards the leads pass through holes; on surface-mount boards tiny parts sit on pads on the surface. The printing on the board names each part: R for a resistor, C for a capacitor, D for a diode, LED, Q for a transistor, F for a fuse, T for a transformer and IC or U for a chip.

blocks.p: Read from the end away from the gold or silver band. On a four-band resistor the first two bands are digits, the third is the multiplier and the fourth is the tolerance. **Examples:** brown, green, red, gold = 15 × 100 = 1500 Ω (1.5 kΩ) ±5%. Orange, white, brown, gold = 39 × 10 = 390 Ω ±5%. Yellow, violet, orange = 47 × 1000 = 47 kΩ. On a five-band resistor the first three bands are digits: brown, black, black, brown, brown = 100 × 10 = 1 kΩ ±1%.

blocks.note: A resistor that reads within its tolerance is good: a 1 kΩ ±5% resistor may read anything from 950 Ω to 1050 Ω. If the body is burnt, replace it, and find out what made it overheat.

blocks.note: Most modern chargers and adapters are **switch-mode** power supplies. They have no large mains transformer: they rectify the mains directly, and their main capacitor charges to about 150 V DC on a 110 V supply (about 310 V on 220 V) and can stay charged after unplugging. At Level 2, do not work inside one unless your instructor tells you to and shows you how to discharge it.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: Diodes, LEDs, electrolytic capacitors, transistors, chips (ICs) and batteries must go in the right way round. Note or photograph the old part's direction before you remove it. A chip has a notch or dot at pin 1.
A reversed electrolytic capacitor can overheat, bulge and burst. Replace a capacitor with one of the same µF value and the same or a higher voltage rating, and check that it fits the space.

Chips and transistors can be damaged by static from your body, which you may not even feel. Wear an anti-static wrist strap connected to the bench's earth point, keep parts in their anti-static bags until needed, and hold them by the body, not the pins.

blocks.p: Soldering joins a component lead to a pad with a melted alloy, solder, that wets both metals and sets as it cools. A good joint conducts well and is strong. A bad joint is the most common cause of faults in battery-powered circuits.

head: Item
Notes
rows: Soldering iron or station
About 25–60 W for electronics, with temperature control if possible. The tip is often set at about 320–370 °C; follow the Centre's setting and the solder maker.
Stand and tip cleaner
A damp (not wet) sponge or brass wool. Keep the tip clean and tinned (coated with a thin layer of solder).
Solder
Flux-cored wire. Leaded solder (such as 60/40 tin-lead) melts at about 183–190 °C. Lead-free solder melts at about 217–227 °C and needs a hotter tip.
Flux
Cleans the metal so that the solder can wet it. Solder wire has a core of rosin flux; extra flux comes as a pen or paste.
Desoldering pump and braid
For removing solder: the pump sucks melted solder away; the copper braid soaks it up.
Hand tools
Flush side cutters, long-nose pliers, tweezers, a magnifier, and pliers or a clip to act as a heat sink.
Safety items
Safety glasses, and fume extraction or good ventilation.

blocks.h: Making a joint on a through-hole board

flow: Clean the pad and the lead; fit the part the right way round and bend its legs slightly to hold it
Wipe the tip and add a little fresh solder to it
Touch the tip to the pad and the lead together for one or two seconds
Feed solder into the joint, where the lead meets the pad, not onto the iron
Take the solder away, then the iron
Keep the joint still for a few seconds while it sets
Trim the lead just above the joint and inspect it

head: Joint
What it looks like
Cause
Cure
rows: Good
Smooth and shiny (lead-free solder is a little duller), shaped like a small cone with sides that curve inwards; the pad is covered and the lead's outline shows
Clean metal, the right heat and the right amount of solder
Nothing needed
Dry (cold) joint
Dull, grainy or lumpy, perhaps with a crack or dark ring round the lead
Too little heat, dirty metal, or the joint moved as it set
Remove the old solder, clean, and resolder with fresh flux
Too much solder
A ball on the pad that hides the lead
Too much solder fed in
Remove the extra with braid: a ball can hide a dry joint underneath
Too little solder
The pad is not fully covered; a gap round the lead
Solder taken away too soon
Reheat and add a little more
Bridge
Solder joining two pads or tracks
Too much solder, or the iron dragged across
Remove it with braid, then check with the ohmmeter
Overheated
Burnt board, lifted pad or track
Iron too hot or held on too long
Repair the track as the instructor shows; work faster next time

flow: Power off: battery out, capacitors discharged
Note the part's direction and value
Heat the joint until the solder melts
Take the solder away with the pump (cock it, place the nozzle on the melted solder, press the button) or with braid pressed under the tip
Repeat for each leg until the leads are free
Lift the part out gently: never pull it while solder still holds it
Clean the holes and pads ready for the new part

ul: Use a clean end of braid each time, and cut off the used part.
If a leg will not come free, add a little fresh solder first and then remove it again: new solder with fresh flux melts and flows more easily.
Pulling hard, or heating for too long, lifts the copper pad and track off the board.

blocks.note: The tip is hot enough to burn you badly and to start a fire. Always return the iron to its stand, never lay it on the bench, and switch it off when you leave. Do not flick solder off the tip. Keep your face out of the fumes: flux fumes can cause asthma. Wash your hands after soldering, and never eat or drink at the bench.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.note: For heat-sensitive parts such as LEDs and transistors, grip the lead between the joint and the body with long-nose pliers, which carry heat away, and keep each joint short.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Testing the repair, the customer and records

ul: All screws, covers, guards, insulating sheets and sleeves are back in place.
Nothing is loose inside: no off-cuts, screws or solder blobs. Shake the item gently and listen.
Internal wires are routed away from hot parts and sharp edges and held in their clips.
The cord grip clamps the outer sheath, and the plug is sound and correctly wired.

blocks.h: Dead tests on a repaired mains appliance

head: Test
How
A pass
rows: Visual check
Look over the whole item, inside and out, before you close it
No damage, nothing loose
Earth continuity (metal-cased, Class I)
A low-resistance ohmmeter between the plug's earth pin and bare metal on the case, while you flex the cord
A very low reading, a fraction of an ohm; the Centre's sheet gives the limit
Insulation resistance
500 V DC between line and neutral joined together and the earth pin or case, with the appliance's switch ON
High: at least the Centre's pass figure, often 1 MΩ (2 MΩ is common for double-insulated items); good items usually read far more
Function checks done dead
Element or load resistance at the plug pins with the switch ON; switch and thermostat continuity
The values you expect

blocks.p: Only when every dead test passes is the appliance given a **function test**, by the instructor or another competent person, on the Centre's protected test bench. They check that it works, that it does not trip the protective device, that its current or power is about right, and that the thermostat switches.

ul: Check the board for solder bridges and for parts fitted the wrong way round.
Before you connect the battery, measure the resistance across the battery clip with the item's switch on. A reading near 0 Ω means there is a short circuit.
Connect the battery with the right **polarity**: red to +, black to −. A reversed battery can destroy diodes, LEDs, capacitors and chips.
Then measure voltages, with the meter in parallel: across the battery, and across the parts.

flow: Receive the item: record the customer's name and phone number, the item, its model and serial number, any accessories, and the fault in their words; give a job number
Find the fault
Tell the customer what is wrong, what the repair will cost and how long it will take
Let the customer decide, and do no extra work without their agreement
Repair and test
Hand over: explain what was done and how to use the item safely; return the old parts if the customer asks

head: Situation
What to do
rows: The repair would cost more than a new item, or nearly as much
Explain the costs and let the customer decide. For example, a new element and labour at J$5,800 for an iron that costs J$5,000 new is not worth doing.
The item is unsafe to repair: a melted case, a rusted-through body, cracked insulation all over
Explain why, advise the customer not to use it, and recommend disposal as e-waste.
The item is still under the maker's warranty
Tell the customer: opening it may end the warranty, and the seller may repair it free.
The fault came from misuse (boiled dry, wrong voltage, pulled by the cord)
Explain politely how to avoid it next time.

ul: The job number, the date, and the customer's and the item's details
The fault as the customer described it
The tests made and their results
The fault found and its cause
The parts used, with their ratings, and the time taken
The final test results: earth continuity, insulation resistance and the function test
Who did the work and who checked it
Return tools and meters. Switch off the soldering iron and leave it in its stand to cool.
Sweep up off-cuts of wire and component leads: they are sharp.
Old circuit boards, cords, parts and batteries are **e-waste**. Put them in the Centre's e-waste collection. Never burn them, put them in the general rubbish or dump them in a gully.
Keep used batteries separate, with their terminals taped, and never put them in a fire.

blocks.note: Burning old cords and boards to recover the copper, which still happens in some places, gives off poisonous smoke. Hand e-waste to the Centre's collection or an approved collector.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can make an appliance safe before I open it, and say which items I must not open.
I can say which tests I may do myself and which the instructor does on the protected test bench.
I can use Ohm's law and the power formula, and work out what an element should read with R = V × V ÷ P.
I can name the kinds of fault: open circuit, short circuit, earth fault, high-resistance joint, intermittent and failed part.
I can set a multimeter, connect it correctly for voltage, current and resistance, and read OL and the prefixes m, k and M.
I can explain why the red lead must go back to the VΩ socket after a current measurement.
I can carry out an insulation resistance test safely, under supervision, and judge the result.
I can follow the fault-finding steps and use the half-split method.
I can find an intermittent fault in a cord or a joint.
I can test a cord, switch, thermostat, thermal fuse and element dead, and choose a correct replacement.
I can replace a power cord with the cord grip on the sheath and the earth conductor a little longer.
I can read a resistor colour code and test resistors, diodes, LEDs and capacitors.
I can describe a simple power supply and its common faults.
I can desolder a part without lifting the tracks and make a good soldered joint.
I can recognise dry joints, bridges and other bad joints and put them right.
I can test a repaired appliance before its function test, and connect a battery with the right polarity.
I can explain a fault and its cost to a customer and complete the repair record.
I can dispose of e-waste and batteries correctly.

head: Figure
What it is
rows: 110 V and 220 V, 50 Hz
The JPS supply
R = V × V ÷ P
What an element should read: 110 V, 1000 W gives about 12 Ω
Prefixes
About 0.5–0.7 V one way, OL the other
A good silicon diode on diode test
About 1.6–2 V one way, OL the other
A good red LED on diode test
500 V DC
The usual insulation test voltage for 110 V and 220 V appliances
Often 1 MΩ
A common minimum insulation reading; follow the Centre's sheet
A fraction of an ohm
A good earth continuity reading on an appliance
Gold ±5%, silver ±10%
Resistor tolerance bands
Often 320–370 °C
A typical soldering iron tip setting

terms: Bimetallic strip
Two metals bonded together that bend when heated; used in many thermostats.
Bridge
Solder that joins two pads or tracks that should be separate.
Continuity
A complete path for current; checked with the meter's beeper or ohms range.
Dead test
A test made with the item disconnected from every supply.
Diode
A part that lets current flow one way only.
Dry joint
A poor soldered joint, dull and grainy, where the solder has not bonded properly; a common cause of intermittent faults.
E-waste
Old electrical and electronic items, boards and batteries, which need special disposal.
Earth continuity test
A test that the metal case of an appliance is joined to the plug's earth pin by a very low resistance.
Flux
A substance that cleans metal so that solder can wet it; inside solder wire as a core.
Half-split method
Testing at the middle of a circuit, then at the middle of the faulty half, and so on.
Insulation resistance
The resistance between live parts and earth or the case; it should be high.
Intermittent fault
A fault that comes and goes.
OL
'Over limit': the meter cannot measure the value, usually because there is an open circuit.
Open circuit
A break in the path of the current.
Polarity
Which way round a part, battery or connection goes: positive and negative, or line and neutral.
Printed circuit board (PCB)
A board that holds electronic parts and joins them with copper tracks.
Rectifier
Diodes that change AC into DC.
Short circuit
A fault where conductors touch so that the current bypasses the load.
Thermal fuse
A one-time device that opens for good when an appliance gets too hot.
Thermostat
A device that keeps a temperature near its setting by switching the heat on and off.
Tolerance
How far a part's real value may be from its marked value, such as ±5%.
Tracks
The thin copper paths on a circuit board that join the parts.

c1.title: A rice cooker that will not heat
c1.text: Mr Lloyd Thompson brings his rice cooker to the Centre's repair bench in Old Harbour, St Catherine. Its plate reads 110 V, 50/60 Hz, 500 W. He says it stopped while the pot was boiling dry, and there was a hot smell. Trainee Kadeem unplugs it and keeps the plug on the bench. The 'warm' lamp does not light, the cord and plug look sound, and under the base he finds a thermal fuse marked 'Tf 184 °C, 10 A, 250 V' in a sleeve beside the heating plate.

c2.title: A new cord for a deep fryer
c2.text: Mrs Joan Reid runs a cook shop in Christiana, Manchester. Her 110 V, 1500 W deep fryer has a stainless steel body and a three-core cord with a three-pin plug. The cord was cut by the lid hinge, close to where it enters the body. Trainee Shamar must fit a new cord and test the fryer before his instructor gives it a function test. The Centre's pass figure for insulation resistance is 1 MΩ.

c3.title: A keyboard adapter with no output
c3.text: Brother Neville brings the power adapter for his church's electronic keyboard to the Centre in Spanish Town, St Catherine. It plugs into a 110 V outlet and should give 12 V DC. Inside are a glass fuse, a small transformer, four diodes in a bridge, a large electrolytic capacitor marked 2200 µF 25 V, and a regulator chip. The fuse glass is blackened inside, and the top of the capacitor has bulged. Trainee Ricardo is doing the repair.

c4.title: A portable radio that cuts out
c4.text: Miss Petrina Gayle in Morant Bay, St Thomas, has a portable radio that runs on four 1.5 V AA cells. It cuts out when it is moved or tapped, then comes back. Trainee Tevin takes out the cells and opens it. Under a magnifier he sees a dull, grainy joint with a dark ring round the lead, where the wire from a battery spring meets the board. There is white crusty powder on one battery spring.

c5.title: Three jobs at a Montego Bay repair shop
c5.text: Trainee Jodian works with Mr Dwight Lewis, a technician, at a small repair shop in Montego Bay, St James. Three items come in on the same morning: a steam iron that leaks water and trips the GFCI in its owner's kitchen, a microwave oven that has stopped heating, and a blender whose owner says it smelt of burning before it stopped.

questions.q: If the heating element is good, about what resistance should Kadeem read across it?
o: About 24 Ω
About 0.22 Ω
About 240 Ω
About 4.5 Ω
questions.why: Use R = V × V ÷ P: 110 × 110 ÷ 500 = 12 100 ÷ 500 ≈ 24 Ω, and a cold element may read a little lower. 4.5 is the current in amps (500 ÷ 110), not the resistance.

questions.q: The element reads 23 Ω, the cord and switch test good, and the thermal fuse reads OL. Before he fits a new thermal fuse, what else must Kadeem find out?
o: Why the heat did not cut off when the pot ran dry
Whether the element reads lower once it is warm
Whether the lamp in the warm circuit has blown
Whether a larger thermal fuse would fit the sleeve
questions.why: The thermal fuse opened because the cooker overheated. Unless the part that should have cut the heat (the thermostat or the cook/warm switch) is tested and the cause found, the new fuse will open again, or the cooker could overheat further.

questions.q: Which part should Kadeem fit in place of the thermal fuse that opened?
o: A 10 A glass fuse in a holder
questions.why: The new thermal fuse must match the old one's operating temperature and current rating. A higher temperature lets the cooker get hotter before it opens; a lower current rating may open in normal use; a glass fuse senses current, not heat.

questions.q: How should the new thermal fuse be connected?
o: Soldered straight to the wires, with a hot iron
With crimp connectors and its heat-resistant sleeve
Clamped under the element's terminal screw
Twisted onto the wires, then wrapped in plastic tape
questions.why: The heat of a soldering iron can open a thermal fuse before it is even in use, so these fuses are crimped with the correct connectors. Tape softens near a heating plate, and the sleeve keeps the fuse insulated from the metal.

questions.q: Which new cord should Shamar fit?
o: A two-core cord of the same size, since the fryer has a switch
Any three-core cord, as long as its colours match the old one
A thinner three-core cord, as it bends more easily at the hinge
A three-core cord with the same or a higher current rating
questions.why: The metal body must stay earthed, so the cord needs three cores. A 1500 W fryer draws about 14 A on 110 V (1500 ÷ 110), so a thinner cord could overheat. Colours say nothing about the current rating.

questions.q: How should Shamar leave the earth conductor where it connects inside the fryer?
o: A little longer than line and neutral
A little shorter than line and neutral
Folded back under the cord grip
Twisted round the line conductor
questions.why: If the cord is ever pulled hard, the shorter line and neutral pull tight and break first, and the earth is the last to come off. The body then stays earthed for as long as possible.

questions.q: Shamar tests from the plug's earth pin to the fryer body. Which reading shows a good earth path?
o: OL
2.5 MΩ
questions.why: The earth path should be a very low resistance, a fraction of an ohm, so that a fault to the body makes the breaker trip. OL means the earth is broken; tens of ohms means a poor connection; megohms is an insulation reading, not a conductor.

questions.q: In the insulation resistance test, the fryer reads 0.3 MΩ from line and neutral to the earth pin. What should happen next?
o: Plug it in for an hour to dry it, then return it
It passes, since any reading above zero is safe enough
Repeat the test at a lower voltage until it passes
It fails; find the leak, such as water in the element
questions.why: 0.3 MΩ is below the 1 MΩ pass figure, so current can leak from the live parts to the body. Fryer elements can let in moisture or grease at their ends. Find and cure the fault; never plug in a failed item to 'dry it out'.

questions.q: What does the blackened glass of the fuse tell Ricardo?
o: The keyboard drew too little current through it
A heavy fault current, such as a short, blew it
It wore out slowly through age and normal use
The fuse was rated far too high for the adapter
questions.why: A fuse that opens on a heavy short circuit melts violently and blackens or silvers the glass. A gentle overload usually leaves a clean break in the wire. A blackened fuse tells you to look for a shorted part before you fit a new one.

questions.q: Before Ricardo touches the board, what must he do about the large capacitor?
o: Wait a few seconds, then touch the legs to check it
Short its two legs together with a screwdriver blade
Discharge it with the resistor tool, then check it
Nothing more, as unplugging removes all the voltage
questions.why: A large capacitor can hold its charge after the adapter is unplugged. The resistor tool drains it safely, and a check on DC volts proves it is empty. Shorting it with a screwdriver makes a flash that can pit the tool, damage the capacitor and burn you.

questions.q: On diode test, one diode reads 0.00 in both directions. The other three read about 0.55 V one way and OL the other. What does this show?
o: One diode is shorted; the other three are good
All four are good, as each one gave a reading
One diode is open; the other three are shorted
One diode is good; the other three are open
questions.why: A good silicon diode reads about 0.5 to 0.7 V one way and OL the other; near zero both ways is a short. A shorted bridge diode short-circuits the transformer on every other half-cycle, which is what blew the fuse. Replace it and the bulged capacitor, and check the other parts for damage from the heavy current.

questions.q: Which capacitor should Ricardo fit in place of the bulged one?
o: 220 µF 25 V, with its stripe on the same side
2200 µF 16 V, as a smaller one fits more easily
2200 µF 35 V, with its stripe on the same side
4700 µF 6.3 V, as a larger value smooths better
questions.why: Keep the same capacitance and use the same or a higher voltage rating, fitted the same way round. 16 V is too close to the voltage across this capacitor and 6.3 V is far below it, and 220 µF is a tenth of the value and would not smooth the DC. Check that the new one fits the space.

questions.q: What kind of fault does Tevin most likely have?
o: An intermittent fault at the cracked joint
An open circuit from a burnt-out resistor
A short circuit from a solder bridge at the joint
An earth fault from the radio's metal case
questions.why: A dull, grainy joint with a ring round the lead is a dry (cracked) joint. It makes contact only some of the time, so the radio cuts out when it is moved or tapped: a classic intermittent fault.

questions.q: How should Tevin repair the joint?
o: Hold the iron on the old joint until the flux starts to smoke
Glue the wire to the pad so that it cannot move any more
Clear the old solder, clean, then remake it with fresh solder
Build a large ball of new solder over the top of the old joint
questions.why: A dry joint is cured by removing the old solder, cleaning the metal and making a new joint with fresh flux-cored solder. A ball on top can hide the crack underneath, overheating lifts the pad, and glue does not conduct.

questions.q: What should Tevin do about the white powder on the battery spring?
o: Rinse the radio under the tap so that the powder dissolves
Clean it off, then check the spring's continuity
Spray it with oil so that the spring will not rust again
Leave it, as the powder cannot affect the radio's sound
questions.why: The powder is residue from a leaking battery, and it corrodes contacts and wires. Clean it off as the instructor shows (often with isopropyl alcohol, a small brush and gloves), check that the contact still conducts, and advise Miss Gayle to take the cells out when the radio is stored.

questions.q: After resoldering, Tevin sees a fine thread of solder joining the new joint to the track beside it. What is it, and what should he do?
o: A heat sink; leave it to cool the joint
A dry joint; add more solder to cover it
A wire link; leave it, as the maker fitted it
A bridge; remove it with desoldering braid
questions.why: Solder joining two tracks that should be separate is a bridge: a short circuit that can damage the radio when the cells go in. Remove it with braid, then check with the ohmmeter that the two tracks are no longer joined.

questions.q: Jodian offers to open the microwave oven and test its parts. What should Mr Lewis tell her?
o: Go ahead, but keep its door open while testing
Go ahead, as long as it is unplugged first
Leave it; its capacitor can hold a deadly charge
Leave it, since a microwave can never be repaired
questions.why: A microwave oven has a high-voltage capacitor that can hold a charge of thousands of volts after the oven is unplugged, enough to kill. Microwave repairs are for trained, authorised technicians, not Level 2 trainees, even with the plug out.

questions.q: The iron trips the GFCI. With the iron unplugged, which test is most likely to find the fault?
o: Continuity of each conductor of the cord, end to end
Insulation resistance from live parts to the soleplate
Resistance of the element, compared with its rated value
Continuity of the thermostat at its very lowest setting
questions.why: A GFCI trips when current leaks to earth. Water from the leaking tank can reach the element terminals and make a leakage path to the metal soleplate, which an insulation resistance test shows as a low reading. Continuity and element tests would not show it.

questions.q: Before quoting for a new blender motor, why should Jodian ask how the blender was used?
o: So she can leave out the dead tests on the new motor
Because motors never fail unless they are misused
So she can choose a smaller motor for the next job
So the same misuse does not burn out the new motor
questions.why: A motor that smelt of burning may have been overloaded, run too long with thick mixtures or jammed. Knowing this lets her check for a cause, such as a seized blade bearing, and advise the owner, so that the new motor lasts.

questions.q: A resistor on a board has the bands orange, white, red, gold. What value should it read, and within what tolerance?
o: 39 Ω, within ±5%
3.9 kΩ, within ±5%
3.9 kΩ, within ±10%
392 Ω, within ±5%
questions.why: Orange is 3 and white is 9, giving 39; red is the multiplier × 100, so the value is 3900 Ω = 3.9 kΩ. Gold is ±5%, so a good resistor reads from about 3.7 kΩ to 4.1 kΩ with one leg lifted.
